title: Extensive subdural spread of a glioblastoma associated with subdural hygroma: case report
case_prompt:
A 67-year-old man presented with progressive fatigue, memory and concentration loss, right-sided neglect, right-sided weakness, and gait disturbance.  
Brain MRI showed an inhomogeneous, contrast-enhancing mass in the left temporo–parieto–occipital region invading the trigone of the left lateral ventricle. He underwent subtotal resection under 5-ALA fluorescence; a small ventricular remnant was left. Histologic analysis revealed glioblastoma multiforme (WHO grade IV). No molecular studies were performed.  
Postoperatively, he received fractionated radiotherapy (62 Gy) with concomitant temozolomide (75 mg/m2 daily for 44 days). Ten weeks after surgery, he experienced vertigo and a transient episode of right visual field restriction and neglect, which resolved with oral corticosteroids. MRI at that time demonstrated new contrast enhancement around the resection cavity, thought to be treatment-related, and a 14-mm-thick left subdural fluid collection causing a 6-mm midline shift. This was interpreted as a subdural hygroma or hematoma.  
One week later, CT showed slight progression of the collection. Burr-hole evacuation yielded a slightly xanthochromic, pressurized subdural hygroma; the dura appeared normal. Three weeks after evacuation, CT again showed recurrence of the subdural collection, which was attributed to post-radiation changes. The patient remained asymptomatic and received two cycles of adjuvant temozolomide (150 mg/m2 and 200 mg/m2).  
Fifteen weeks after tumour resection (four weeks after the first hygroma evacuation), he returned with concentration loss, fatigue, and moderate right hemiparesis. CT revealed a markedly progressive subdural fluid collection with a 3-mm-thick subdural membrane. A second burr-hole evacuation was performed, but drainage remained unsatisfactory and a subduro–peritoneal shunt was placed. A thick greyish subdural membrane was observed intraoperatively, but no tissue was sampled. Although the fluid volume decreased, significant mass effect persisted.  
Several days later, MRI performed as part of tumor follow-up showed an inhomogeneous, contrast-enhancing subdural membrane with irregular contours over the left hemisphere.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Initial interpretation as a benign subdural collection — “which was interpreted as a subdural hygroma or hematoma.”  
2. Recurrence attributed to treatment effects rather than neoplasm — “This finding was considered to be related to post-radiation changes.”  
3. Imaging raised suspicion for tumor involvement of the subdural space — “Subdural spread of the glioblastoma was suspected, which was validated by an open tissue biopsy.”  
4. Secondary gliosarcoma transformation was considered on pathology review — “Our reference pathology centre considered gliosarcoma as a differential diagnosis.”
